scope: Frozen Physics 10 full export, 2026-09-27; 100 distinct definitions: 11 lecture, 14 homework, 53 timed multiple-choice, 5 timed essay, 17 take-home variants. IDs are export-local locators, not live database IDs.

exercises.text: Give two examples of a physical property that is quantized. For each property, describe its allowed values.
Give two examples of a physical property that is not quantized. For each property, describe the continuous range of values it can take.
What aspect of the blackbody spectrum forced Planck to propose quantization of energy levels in the thermal oscillators?
Why don’t we notice quantization in everyday events?

A LiBr molecule oscillates with a frequency of 1.7×1013 Hz. (a) What is the difference in energy in eV between allowed oscillator states? (b) What is the approximate value of n for a state having an energy of 1.0 eV?
The difference in energy between allowed oscillator states in HBr molecules is 0.330 eV. What is the oscillation frequency of this molecule?

What determines whether electromagnetic radiation can eject electrons from a particular material? Explain how this affects which parts of the electromagnetic spectrum can produce the photoelectric effect in that material.
Which aspects of the photoelectric effect cannot be explained without photons? Which can be explained without photons? Are the latter inconsistent with the existence of photons?
What is the longest wavelength of EM radiation that can eject a photoelectron from a silver surface with a work function of 4.73 eV? Is this in the visible range?
Find the longest wavelength of EM radiation that can eject an electron from a potassium surface with a work function of 2.30 eV. Is this visible EM radiation?
What is the work function in eV of a magnesium surface if the longest wavelength that can eject electrons is 337 nm?
Calculate the work function in eV of an aluminum surface if the longest wavelength that can eject electrons is 304 nm.
What is the maximum kinetic energy in eV of electrons ejected by 450-nm EM radiation from a sodium surface with a work function of 2.28 eV?
UV radiation with a wavelength of 120 nm falls on a gold surface with a work function of 4.82 eV. What is the maximum kinetic energy in eV of the ejected photoelectrons?
Violet light of wavelength 400 nm ejects electrons with a maximum kinetic energy of 0.820 eV from a sodium surface. What is the work function of this surface?
UV radiation with a wavelength of 300 nm falls on a uranium surface, ejecting electrons with a maximum kinetic energy of 0.500 eV. What is the work function of this surface?
What is the wavelength of EM radiation that ejects electrons with a maximum kinetic energy of 2.00 eV from a calcium surface with a work function of 2.87 eV? What type of EM radiation is this?
Find the wavelength of photons that eject electrons with a maximum kinetic energy of 0.100 eV from a potassium surface with a work function of 2.30 eV. Are these photons visible?

A laser beam delivers 2.00 mW of power at a wavelength of 400 nm to a calcium surface with a work function of 2.87 eV. (a) Find the ideal upper limit on the number of electrons ejected per second, assuming that every incident photon ejects one electron. (b) Find the ideal upper limit on the power carried away as electron kinetic energy, additionally assuming that every emitted electron has the maximum kinetic energy.

(a) How is the interference pattern produced by electrons similar to that produced by water waves? (b) Compare how the two patterns are observed. When electrons are sent through the apparatus one at a time, what is detected for each electron, and how does the interference pattern emerge after many electrons have been detected?

(a) Describe an experimental observation that supports the wave nature of matter. (b) Describe an experimental observation that supports the particle nature of electromagnetic radiation. For each observation, explain how it supports the corresponding description.

(a) At what speed would an electron have a de Broglie wavelength of 1.00 mm? (b) Calculate the speed of an electron with a de Broglie wavelength of 1.00 μm. Through what potential difference must an electron be accelerated from rest to reach the speed in part (b)?
What is the wavelength of an electron moving at 3.00% of the speed of light?

(a) Using the nonrelativistic relation p=mv, calculate the speed of a proton with a de Broglie wavelength of 6.00 fm, approximately a nuclear length scale. (b) Repeat the calculation for an electron with the same wavelength. Compare both results with the speed of light. For which particle is the nonrelativistic approximation reasonable? Explain. (1fm=10−15m.)
A pool ball has a mass of 0.170 kg and a radius of 2.86 cm. At what speed would its de Broglie wavelength equal its radius?
Experiments are performed with ultracold neutrons having velocities as small as 1.00 m/s. (a) What is the wavelength of such a neutron? (b) What is its kinetic energy in eV?
What is the wavelength of an electron accelerated through a 30.0-kV potential, as in a TV tube?
What is the kinetic energy of an electron in a TEM having a 0.0100-nm wavelength?

The velocity of a proton emerging from a Van de Graaff accelerator is 25.0% of the speed of light. (a) What is the proton’s wavelength? (b) What is its kinetic energy, assuming it is nonrelativistic? (c) What was the equivalent voltage through which it was accelerated?

An electron accelerated in an X-ray tube has a kinetic energy of 100 keV. (a) Using the nonrelativistic approximation, estimate its de Broglie wavelength. (b) What is the shortest wavelength of an X-ray photon that can be produced if all of the electron’s kinetic energy is transferred to a single photon? Compare this wavelength with the electron’s wavelength from part (a).

(a) State the Heisenberg uncertainty principle for position and momentum, and explain what each uncertainty represents. (b) Does this principle impose a universal lower limit on position uncertainty, such as 10−10m (an atomic scale), 10−15m (a nuclear scale), or some other fixed length? Explain. (c) If neither position uncertainty nor momentum uncertainty has a fixed lower limit by itself, what does the principle constrain about how precisely both can be known simultaneously?

An electron is localized with a position uncertainty of 0.100 nm, approximately an atomic length scale. (a) Using the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, calculate the minimum uncertainty in its velocity. (b) Estimate the kinetic-energy scale associated with this localization using K=12me(Δv)2. Express your answer in electron volts. (c) Compare this energy scale with 4.48 eV, the energy required to separate a hydrogen molecule into two hydrogen atoms. Is it small enough to neglect when considering energies involved in molecular bonding?

In Millikan’s oil-drop experiment, one looks at a small oil drop held motionless between two plates. Take the voltage between the plates to be 2033 V, and the plate separation to be 2.00 cm. The oil drop (of density 0.81g/cm3) has a diameter of 4.0×10−6 m. Find the charge on the drop, in terms of electron units.

What two measured quantities allowed the first calculation of me, the mass of the electron? (a) The ratios qe/me and qp/mp. (b) The values of qe and EB. (c) The ratio qe/me and qe. Explain how the two quantities you selected can be combined to calculate the electron’s mass. Which of these quantities did Thomson measure in his cathode-ray experiments?
Rutherford found the size of the nucleus to be about 10−15 m. This implied a huge density. What would this density be for gold?
An aspiring physicist wants to build a scale model of a hydrogen atom for her science fair project. If the atom is 1.00 m in diameter, how big should she try to make the nucleus?
How do the allowed orbits for electrons in atoms differ from the allowed orbits for planets around the sun? Explain how the correspondence principle applies here.
(a) Calculate the wavelengths of the first and third lines in the Lyman series. (b) In which region of the electromagnetic spectrum do these wavelengths lie?
What is the smallest-wavelength line in the Balmer series? Is it in the visible part of the spectrum?
Show that the entire Paschen series is in the infrared part of the spectrum. To do this, you only need to calculate the shortest wavelength in the series.
Do the Balmer and Lyman series overlap? To answer this, calculate the shortest-wavelength Balmer line and the longest-wavelength Lyman line.
Look up the values of the quantities in aB=h24π2mekqe2, and verify that the Bohr radius aB is 0.529×10−10 m.
Verify that the ground state energy E0 is 13.6 eV by using E0=2π2qe4mek2h2.
If a hydrogen atom has its electron in the n=4 state, how much energy in eV is needed to ionize it?
A hydrogen atom in an excited state can be ionized with less energy than when it is in its ground state. What is n for a hydrogen atom if 0.850 eV of energy can ionize it?
Find the radius of a hydrogen atom in the n=2 state according to Bohr’s theory.
Show that 13.6eVhc=1.097×107m−1=R (Rydberg’s constant), as discussed in the text.
A wavelength of 4.653μm is observed in a hydrogen spectrum for a transition that ends in the nf=5 level. What was ni for the initial level of the electron?
How is the de Broglie wavelength of electrons related to the quantization of their orbits in atoms and molecules?

candidates.coverage_gap: Retained question fs-id1559465 asks generally about classical versus photon explanations; no explicit controlled-change prediction distinguishes emission rate from maximum kinetic energy.
candidates.proposed_wording: Monochromatic light ejects electrons from a metal surface. (a) If the light intensity increases while its frequency stays fixed, what happens to the number of electrons emitted per second and their maximum kinetic energy? (b) If the frequency increases, what happens to the maximum kinetic energy? Explain both answers using the photon model.
candidates.expected_reasoning: At fixed frequency, photon energy is unchanged; increased photon arrival rate increases emission rate under the ordinary single-photon model. Maximum kinetic energy is unchanged in (a), increases in (b). Do not infer an emission-rate change from frequency alone.

candidates.proposed_wording: For hydrogen, E_n = -13.6 eV/n^2. (a) Calculate the energies of the n = 2 and n = 4 states and sketch their positions on an energy-level diagram. Mark the transition from n = 4 to n = 2. (b) Find the energy of the emitted photon. (c) Find its frequency and wavelength. Explain why the photon’s energy equals the difference between the two levels rather than either level’s energy alone.
candidates.expected_reasoning: E_2 = -3.40 eV; E_4 = -0.850 eV. Downward transition emits 2.55 eV, approximately 6.17e14 Hz and 486 nm. Conservation of energy gives the level difference; negative bound-state energies are measured relative to the ionization reference.
candidates.implementation: Add after the retained Bohr energy/ionization questions. Use textbook constants; allow rounding. Fixed n = 4 to n = 2 avoids assuming every randomized Balmer transition is visible.

source_issues.issue: Take-home solution repeats a statement from an INCORRECT-statement multiple-choice item as if correct: classical theory agrees at short wavelengths. Do not copy the key.
Take-home key labels 10 microns as microwaves; it is infrared. No adaptation recommended.
Uses Delta x Delta p > h as the keyed uncertainty formula. Do not copy as the exact relation; reconcile with the textbook convention.
Some choices overstate inevitable ejection, completely unrestricted momentum, or location anywhere in the apparatus. Avoid importing these claims.
Control comment assumes n_i = 3 through 7 to n_f = 2 always gives visible light; n_i = 7 lies below 400 nm. Proposed fixed n_i = 4 is unambiguous.
Lecture transcript loosely calls every macroscopic body a blackbody. Do not carry that statement into textbook wording.

summary: Six recommended adaptations: five new exercises and one stopping-potential extension of an existing exercise. Two optional lower-priority conceptual questions. No new hydrogen-like-ion, energy-time, relativistic, laser, or Fourier-analysis requirements.
